claims.text: Low hardness and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by its homogeneous single-phase solid-solution state permitting unimpeded dislocation glide.
Transformation-induced obstacles can strengthen high- or medium-entropy alloys without necessarily compromising plasticity.
Precipitation-induced obstacles enhance work hardening in other high- or medium-entropy systems.
Easy dislocation motion produces high plasticity and machinability but limited strain hardening in CoCrFeNiTi.
Equimolar or near-equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can exist as a simple homogeneous FCC or BCC solid solution with minimal microstructural heterogeneity.
A thermal-mechanical treatment or minor compositional modification can induce an FCC-to-HCP transformation or coherent nanoprecipitation in CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed comparison is performed at room temperature under quasi-static tensile or compression loading while the baseline remains single phase.
Absence of deformation-induced transformation or precipitates leaves few phase-boundary or interface obstacles to dislocation motion.
Plastic deformation in single-phase CoCrFeNiTi is dominated by unimpeded dislocation glide on multiple slip systems.
The proposed glide mechanism causes extensive plasticity, low work hardening, high machinability, and reduced hardness and strength.
Untreated CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit low yield strength and hardness together with high ductility.
Introducing a secondary phase or precipitate should increase hardness and yield strength by adding barriers to dislocation motion.
As-cast equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a pure, homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
The proposed findings are limited to near-equimolar compositions, room temperature, and quasi-static loading.
The influence of Ti on stacking-fault energy in this alloy remains unclear.
Short-range ordering may contribute to the mechanical behavior of CoCrFeNiTi.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant strength and hardness increase, or failure to produce the intended barriers, is defined as falsifying the hypothesis.
